no matter how far we are from God, His flame burns in us. So, even if you feel distant and as though God has forgotten you, there remains the flame within. For Dante and our early civilizations, God was eternal love, eternal compassion, and eternal forgiveness. He will never forget you; He will always forgive you. You must believe in God to return to Him. Live a life of righteousness, love, compassion, and imagination if you wish to return to God.

We are here to expand the consciousness of the universe by embracing love and imagining a better world. Now let's ask ourselves this question: If every early religion, whether it be Daoism, Hinduism, the Egyptians, or Native Americans, believed and knew this, how did we come to forget or deny it in light of material reality?

Remember the big bang, evolution, and neuroscience; they taught us that there is no God, no purpose, just randomness and matter. So, how do we get here? The answer is simple: Heaven represents spirituality (consciousness), Earth is mechanical (machines), and Hell lies between them. Our choice through free will determines whether we stay in heaven or descend into hell.

Most of human history has chosen heaven, but eventually, people chose hell. With access to technology from choosing hell, you can conquer others. To control them, you need them to fear death, forget God, and fear death as the worst thing that could happen.

To achieve this, use science like theories of the big bang, evolution, and neuroscience to make people forget their divinity. Science's purpose is to accomplish this. However, eventually, everyone will die, so a new technology called transhumanism was created—surpassing humanity by uploading your brain to the internet for eternal life.

Why are they doing this? Secret societies in power often control mass bureaucracies. Bureaucrats are lazy and would rather do nothing, but as part of secret societies, you can coordinate and maintain secrecy through transgression. If found out, everyone is committed to keeping each other's secrets.
